turns.en: We're in a new era of building applications and things that we couldn't build just a few years ago. We see a lot of companies that need a little bit of help. So we started investing in FDEs a couple years ago, but it's really been this year we've scaled it up a lot. I think we started this year having like four FDEs, now I think we have like 24 or something like that, so we've grown a lot. And they do a lot of heavy customer engagement. They work with a lot of customers on performance tuning, especially with LMs. We see that there's so much benefit from sitting down with customers and training draft models and tweaking parameters and DM and SG lang. They often fix bugs—or not fix bugs, but when customers run into issues, they often work with customers trying to figure out how to work around that. Another thing we've used FDEs a lot for is proactively—if we see certain customers overprovisioning with Modal, like customers requesting too much CPU or too much memory for instance, that's kind of expensive, and we try to catch those things and sit down with those customers like, 'Yo, you're spending a lot of money on Modal right now, we can actually help you save money.' And then of course, with active deals, we help them migrate code from other platforms, things like that.
turns.zh: 我们正处于一个构建应用和几年前无法构建的东西的新时代。我们看到很多公司需要一点帮助。所以我们在几年前开始投资 FDE，但今年我们真正扩大了规模。我记得今年开始时我们有四个 FDE，现在大概有 24 个左右，所以增长了很多。他们做大量的客户互动工作。他们与许多客户合作进行性能调优，尤其是语言模型。我们发现，与客户坐下来训练草稿模型并调整参数、DM 和 SG lang 有很多好处。他们经常修复 bug——或者不是修复 bug，而是当客户遇到问题时，他们经常与客户合作，想办法解决。我们经常使用 FDE 的另一个方面是主动出击——如果我们看到某些客户在 Modal 上过度配置，比如请求过多的 CPU 或内存，这很昂贵，我们试图抓住这些情况，并与这些客户坐下来谈，比如‘嘿，你现在在 Modal 上花了很多钱，我们实际上可以帮助你省钱。’当然，对于活跃的交易，我们帮助他们从其他平台迁移代码等等。

turns.en: I think we never have the intention of becoming a service-heavy business. I think the goal for FDEs is: A, to be a part of the sales process and closing deals; B, to serve customers and do some customer support; but I actually think the most important thing is C, bridging gaps in the product that we later want to turn into real features. So to a large extent, anything an FDE does, my question is always long-term: how do we turn this into product so we don't need an FDE for this?
turns.zh: 我认为我们从未打算成为服务密集型业务。我认为 FDE 的目标是：A，参与销售过程和达成交易；B，服务客户并提供一些客户支持；但我实际上认为最重要的是 C，弥合产品中的差距，我们后来希望将其转化为真正的功能。所以在很大程度上，FDE 做的任何事情，我的问题总是长期来看：我们如何将其转化为产品，这样我们就不需要 FDE 来做这个了？

turns.en: Yeah. Do you guys hire PMs, product managers?
turns.zh: 是的。你们雇佣 PM，产品经理吗？

turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 不。

turns.en: Would you say these FDEs are kind of like pseudo-PMs?
turns.zh: 你会说这些 FDE 有点像伪 PM 吗？

turns.en: It's a little bit of a different function. Certainly on the more customer-facing side they are, but on the more inward internal side, there's a separate part of product management which is more like what are the next building blocks Modal should invest in. And then there's something in between: looking at maybe 10-20 different customers, they're all asking for slightly different things, but what are the patterns? How do we turn this into product? We do have people doing product with us, and it's sort of evolved—we've had people basically become product managers after previously being either dev or engineers, just showing strong aptitude for thinking very strategically about what we have to build. So I'm actually not anti-product management. I do think that a lot of companies in the past hired product managers too eagerly, and I think there's a risk that you can sort of see it in a lot of products—certain products, you can tell there are just eager product managers that thought of widgety things and just shipped them. I think doing product management at an infra company really well is very, very hard because it takes a very deep level of strategic thinking about what are the foundational building blocks, where do we want to be in one to two years, because the truth is building infrastructure is very hard, and how do we make sure we don't end up with 35 features that are kind of similar looking but all do slightly different things. That sort of level of thinking is very rare to find, and for that reason we haven't aggressively tried to build up a product management team yet.
turns.zh: 这是一个有点不同的职能。当然，在更面向客户的一面，他们是，但在更内向的内部一面，产品管理有一个单独的部分，更像是 Modal 接下来应该投资哪些构建模块。然后中间还有一些事情：看看也许 10-20 个不同的客户，他们都要求稍微不同的东西，但模式是什么？我们如何将其转化为产品？我们确实有员工和我们一起做产品，而且它有点进化了——我们有人基本上在之前是开发或工程师之后成为了产品经理，只是在对我们必须构建的东西进行非常战略性的思考方面表现出很强的能力。所以我实际上并不反对产品管理。我确实认为过去很多公司过于急切地雇佣产品经理，我认为存在一种风险，你可以在很多产品中看到——某些产品，你可以看出有急切的产品经理只是想到了一些小部件的东西就发布了。我认为在一家基础设施公司做好产品管理非常非常难，因为这需要非常深入的战略思考，思考什么是基础构建模块，我们在一到两年内想要达到什么位置，因为事实是构建基础设施非常难，以及我们如何确保我们不会最终得到 35 个看起来相似但都做稍微不同事情的功能。那种水平的思考非常罕见，因此我们还没有积极尝试建立产品管理团队。

turns.en: Yeah, that makes sense. How would you say your teams have been evolving maybe since Gen AI? Because I would assume—I mean, you obviously worked at Spotify. You had a certain team structure. Have your team structures evolved a lot now that we have coding agents?
turns.zh: 是的，这说得通。你会说你的团队自 Gen AI 以来如何演变？因为我假设——我的意思是，你显然在 Spotify 工作过。你有一定的团队结构。现在我们有编码代理，你的团队结构变化很大吗？

turns.en: In a funny way, yes, I do think team structures have changed a lot, but I'm actually not convinced it was Gen AI driving that. In particular, one thing I've seen a lot is that there's been a swing back towards being an IC, which I actually think is very, very positive for the space as a whole. If you look back at the space 10 years ago, 20 years ago, everyone wanted to be in management because that was a way you would get more money and more recognition and more prestige. I think that shift actually started even before Gen AI, but I do think it's heavily accelerated with AI. We make it very clear to everyone at Modal that manager and IC—there's no difference in prestige. Everyone is just a member of technical staff. It's about ultimately your contributions. And we see a lot of ex-managers becoming ICs because they want to go back and build code. And there's been a shift away from non-technical managers. Everyone, pretty much including me—I still write a lot of code at Modal and in Oxhat 2—and pretty much everyone in the tech team and a lot of people who are not in the tech team still write code. So that to me is a recent phenomenon, but I actually don't know if it's necessarily caused by Gen AI, but I think Gen AI has greatly accelerated it because it made writing code even easier and lowered the cost.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，是的，我确实认为团队结构变化很大，但我实际上并不确信是 Gen AI 驱动的。特别是，我经常看到的一件事是，有一种回归个人贡献者（IC）的趋势，我实际上认为这对整个领域非常非常积极。如果你回顾 10 年、20 年前的领域，每个人都想进入管理层，因为那是获得更多金钱、更多认可和更多声望的方式。我认为这种转变实际上在 Gen AI 之前就开始了，但我确实认为它随着 AI 而大大加速。我们向 Modal 的每个人明确表示，经理和 IC 在声望上没有区别。每个人都只是技术员工。最终重要的是你的贡献。我们看到很多前经理成为 IC，因为他们想回去写代码。而且有一种远离非技术经理的趋势。几乎每个人，包括我——我仍然在 Modal 和 Oxhat 2 写很多代码——而且技术团队中几乎每个人以及很多非技术团队的人仍然写代码。所以对我来说，这是一个最近的现象，但我实际上不知道它是否一定是 Gen AI 引起的，但我认为 Gen AI 大大加速了它，因为它使写代码更容易，降低了成本。

turns.en: So if you have like non-technical people like committing code like how do you how do you review that like how do you guys do code reviews?
turns.zh: 那么，如果有非技术人员提交代码，你们怎么审查？你们团队如何进行代码审查？

turns.en: We do code reviews but we think of it as optional. I mean for most my view is like code reviews in large part is like people in many cases trying to just escape the accountability of like you know merging things into production and if you have that culture like then to me that's a sign that you need to invest way more in CD and CI and things like that. CI in particular but also CD, continuous integration because it's deployment. We do code reviews like when I write code occasionally I'm asking authors like is this in line with how you think about things? I hope I'm not changing the architecture fundamentally. But we also make it clear internally that code reviews are quite optional. And if you're just changing docs, if you're just doing some basic stuff like don't wait for a human to look at it especially in the era of AI. Why do you need a human to look at every piece of code? You don't have to.
turns.zh: 我们做代码审查，但认为它是可选的。我的观点是，很多时候代码审查只是人们试图逃避将代码合并到生产环境的责任。如果你有那种文化，那对我来说就是一个信号，说明你需要更多地投资于持续交付（CD）和持续集成（CI）之类的东西。特别是 CI，还有 CD，因为它是部署。我们做代码审查，比如我写代码时偶尔会问作者：这符合你的思路吗？我希望我没有从根本上改变架构。但我们也在内部明确表示，代码审查是相当可选的。如果你只是改文档，或者做一些基本的事情，就不要等人工来看，尤其是在 AI 时代。为什么需要人工审查每一段代码？你不必。

turns.en: But that does require you to have very good controls internally around testing for a company.
turns.zh: 但这确实要求公司在测试方面有非常好的内部控制。

turns.en: Yeah. And exactly like infra companies like we need one more nine than the average startup in terms of uptime but these are investments you just have to make. You have to build systems that are very resilient, you have to have rate limits everywhere. You have to decouple systems. You have to make sure that nothing is a single point of failure. They have to have extremely good test coverage. Agents are actually really good at writing tests these days, which was a few years ago I thought like one of the major things missing in agents. Now they're actually quite good at writing tests too because I think it takes a little bit of need to step out of what you're trying to do for a second and be almost a little bit like devil's advocate to write good tests, but now they're actually quite good at writing tests too. So I think all these things help.
turns.zh: 是的。就像基础设施公司，我们的正常运行时间需要比普通初创公司多一个九，但这些是你必须做的投资。你必须构建非常有弹性的系统，到处都要有限流。你必须解耦系统。你必须确保没有单点故障。它们必须有极好的测试覆盖率。现在智能体实际上非常擅长写测试，几年前我认为这是智能体缺失的主要能力之一。现在它们也非常擅长写测试，因为我认为写好的测试需要你暂时跳出正在做的事情，几乎要扮演一点魔鬼代言人的角色，但现在它们在这方面也相当不错了。所以我认为所有这些都有帮助。

turns.en: Do you guys use like frontier models for coding or do you guys have you guys experimented with uh like the open source ones?
turns.zh: 你们用前沿模型来编程吗？还是尝试过开源模型？

turns.en: We experiment with everything but yeah initially was a lot of Cursor then of course Claude and Codex and now a lot of people are using Night Shift and all these open source stuff or other stacks so I don't necessarily have a strong point of view. I want people to experiment and try different things. We use frontier models, use open source models. We're trying to do a little bit more dogfooding internally now that we're actually running inference for a lot of the open source models at a very large scale. I think it's also helpful to use our internal endpoints for a lot of agentic development. So we try to promote that a little bit.
turns.zh: 我们什么都尝试，但最初大量使用 Cursor，然后当然有 Claude 和 Codex，现在很多人使用 Night Shift 和所有这些开源的东西或其他技术栈，所以我没有强烈的观点。我希望人们实验和尝试不同的东西。我们使用前沿模型，也使用开源模型。现在我们实际上正在大规模地为许多开源模型运行推理，我们试图在内部多做一些吃自己的狗粮。我认为对于许多智能体式开发，使用我们的内部端点也很有帮助。所以我们试图稍微推广这一点。

turns.en: Something I read maybe like I don't know a year ago, maybe like two years ago, you were saying that you didn't think that there was going to be like a big on-prem business for you guys. Um, have you maybe like changed your opinion on that?
turns.zh: 我大约一年前或两年前读到你说，你认为你们不会有大的本地部署业务。你改变看法了吗？

turns.en: No, I have not changed my opinion. I think Modal to me I'm a cloud maximalist and maybe to take a step back like when the cloud came in 2008 2009 or whatever my first reaction was like that's crazy like why would I want to take my code and run it on someone else's computer that's like insane and then like 6 months later I was doing it and I think it took me 6 months to change my mind it took probably enterprises like another 15 to 20 years but you look at vendors like Snowflake or I mean AWS and I think there's many examples of Data Dog etc like the cloud is clearly winning and the multi-tenant systems are clearly winning and to me on-prem looks increasingly like sort of a legacy business model and I actually think BYOC, VPC peering, all of these things to me they reflect sort of an outdated security model of like we need to protect everything inside our own network, using the network as a moat and that I don't think is true anything anymore. We've sort of moved on to more robust security paradigms like zero trust and things like that. And so to me the things like they look increasingly as outdated at least from a security perspective from our perspective also like the fact that we have full control over our entire infrastructure stack. We rent all the hardware. We deploy we manage all the infrastructure. We deploy and manage health and observe all the metrics on all the hosts. It means we can iterate very fast and build a greater product and I think that's very valuable versus customers in the past who had enterprise additions that they had to deploy on customers environment. They have to be very they have to think very carefully about release management and having depend like we don't care like if we want to introduce a new database like we can introduce a new database because we have control over it like we don't need to think about what customers have access to. So to me multi-tenency has so many different benefits. I mean that being said if we were to work with some very large Fortune 500 customer in the future and they ask for BYOC we've done this in the past we'll give them a number like that number is very high and no one said yes to it so far but who knows at the right price I would still build it and I think there's maybe separately like another thing which I think is interesting which is like in theory BYOC might also be a way to work with and get capacity in certain ways like we sometimes work with Neolabs and those Neolabs already have very large capacity reservations and the question is like how do we get them to run Modal when they already have capacity and BYOC might be a solution we can still keep the control plane in our environment and the other flip side of that is like we could maybe even run other people's stuff on that capacity so there's some fun stuff you could do in theory where you can sort of aggregate all that capacity into one big pool. We're excited about some of those ideas, but in general, I feel like on-prem I don't know if we're ever going to do, but BYOC like maybe bring your own cloud. I keep saying BC. I should explain acronyms.
turns.zh: 不，我没有改变看法。我认为 Modal 对我来说，我是一个云最大化主义者。也许退一步说，当云在 2008 年或 2009 年出现时，我的第一反应是这太疯狂了，为什么我要把代码放在别人的电脑上运行，这太疯狂了。然后大约 6 个月后我就这么做了。我花了 6 个月改变想法，企业可能又花了 15 到 20 年。但你看像 Snowflake 或 AWS 这样的供应商，还有很多例子如 Data Dog 等，云显然在赢，多租户系统显然在赢。对我来说，本地部署越来越像一种遗留商业模式。我实际上认为 BYOC、VPC 对等连接等所有这些都反映了一种过时的安全模型，即我们需要保护自己网络内的一切，把网络当作护城河，而我认为这不再正确。我们已经转向更强大的安全范式，比如零信任等。所以对我来说，这些东西至少从安全角度看越来越过时。从我们的角度看，我们完全控制整个基础设施栈。我们租用所有硬件。我们部署和管理所有基础设施。我们部署和管理健康状态并观察所有主机上的所有指标。这意味着我们可以快速迭代并构建更好的产品，我认为这非常有价值。相比之下，过去客户有企业版必须部署在客户环境中。他们必须非常仔细地考虑发布管理和依赖关系。而我们不在乎，如果我们想引入新数据库，我们可以引入，因为我们控制它，不需要考虑客户能访问什么。所以对我来说，多租户有很多不同的好处。话虽如此，如果未来我们与一些非常大的财富 500 强客户合作，他们要求 BYOC，我们过去做过，我们会给他们一个价格，那个价格非常高，到目前为止没有人同意，但谁知道呢，如果价格合适，我仍然会构建它。我认为还有另一件有趣的事情，理论上 BYOC 也可能是一种合作和获取容量的方式。我们有时与 Neolabs 合作，那些 Neolabs 已经有非常大的容量预留，问题是如何让他们在已有容量上运行 Modal，BYOC 可能是一个解决方案，我们仍然可以把控制平面留在我们的环境中。另一方面，我们甚至可以在那容量上运行别人的东西，所以理论上你可以做一些有趣的事情，比如把所有容量聚合成一个大池子。我们对一些想法感到兴奋，但总的来说，我觉得本地部署，我不知道我们是否会做，但 BYOC，也许吧，自带云。我一直说 BC，我应该解释缩写。

turns.en: Let's say hypothetically you are going to raise, I should say, more money soon. What would you use that money for?
turns.zh: 假设你即将筹集更多资金，你会用这些钱做什么？

turns.en: Like I mentioned, in this capacity situation, a lot of the money—a lot of the cash flow, I should say, that's required—is capacity prepayments, right? So that to me represents the best use of cash today. We're ramping up capacity very aggressively. Maybe we move into other types of deployment models in the future, ownership or whatever. But I think there's always going to be a cash component of that, like some sort of down payment or prepayment or something like that. So that to me is the greatest use of cash right now. There are of course other things like salaries and office spaces and stuff like that, but in the grand scheme of our financials, that's basically a rounding error right now.
turns.zh: 就像我提到的，在这种产能情况下，所需的大量资金——我应该说大量现金流——是产能预付款，对吧？所以对我来说，这是当前现金的最佳用途。我们正在非常积极地扩大产能。也许未来我们会转向其他类型的部署模式，比如所有权之类的。但我认为总会有现金部分，比如某种首付或预付款之类的。所以对我来说，这是目前现金的最大用途。当然还有其他事情，比如工资和办公空间之类的，但在我们财务的大局中，那现在基本上是个舍入误差。

turns.en: Yeah. Interesting. Do you think that's going to change?
turns.zh: 嗯，有意思。你觉得这种情况会改变吗？

turns.en: No. I think the operating leverage that we have in this business is kind of insane. Like we have 200 employees—they cost a lot of money—but the GPUs cost a lot more money.
turns.zh: 不会。我认为我们在这个业务中的运营杠杆有点疯狂。比如我们有 200 名员工——他们花费很多钱——但 GPU 花费更多钱。

turns.en: If you had to say, what are the top three things that are your biggest focus or the business's biggest focus right now? What would you say those are?
turns.zh: 如果你必须说，你或公司目前最关注的三大重点是什么？你会说是哪些？

turns.en: Capacity and the financial complexity, and in general how do we think about that space, how do we think about pricing and packaging, how do we think about the tension between ownership and renting—should we go in a more neo cloud direction, should we go in the opposite direction, the sort of counter precision—like that's probably the biggest thing that I think a lot about. The second biggest thing I think a lot about is probably around product strategy. I think a lot about what are the next building blocks. If we do more agentic stuff, what are the things we need? Are there certain storage primitives or compute primitives, or in general, what is the thing that the world is going to wake up and realize they need over the next few years, and ideally we have that at that point. We've been pretty good in general at anticipating demand and building products in advance of it with the serverless functions and the sandboxes. So what's the thing? Then I would say the third thing I think a lot about is more around culture and company building and stuff like that. We recently crossed 200 people. We're growing extremely fast. We'll probably hit 250 by the end of the year. When you're growing very fast, you have 250 people that are all trying to figure out how they can add the most value to Modal, and making sure that they have the right context, that they have the right motivation, that they're excited to come into work every day because they get to build something incredibly cool and they know what makes Modal successful and what they can do—aligning the incentives and making sure that people have a very positive culture where they have the implicit trust to do a lot of stuff but also the accountability to deliver the best things and be held accountable if they're not doing it. To me those are super critical things around this scale. When you're 10, 20, 30 people, you can all just sit in a room and it's all implicit and you kind of just feel it. People can read me—they can tell me when I get a little bit annoyed. They can tell when I'm happy. Now we're 250 people and people don't necessarily see it, and of course there are a lot of new people who are maybe a little bit nervous to talk to the CEO and all this stuff. So how do I remain approachable? And there's the Dunbar number, which I think is more faked than anything—at least the story behind it—but it is actually kind of real still, like there's something around 150, 200. We're laying the foundation of the culture, which is very, very important.
turns.zh: 产能和财务复杂性，以及总的来说我们如何思考那个领域，如何思考定价和打包，如何思考所有权和租赁之间的张力——我们应该朝更 neo cloud 的方向发展，还是朝相反的方向，那种 counter precision——这大概是我思考最多的事情。我思考第二多的大概是产品战略。我经常思考下一个构建块是什么。如果我们做更多智能体式的东西，我们需要什么？是否有某些存储原语或计算原语，或者总的来说，世界在未来几年会醒来并意识到他们需要什么，理想情况下我们在那个时候已经有了。我们总体上一直很擅长预测需求并提前构建产品，比如无服务器函数和沙盒。那么那个东西是什么？然后我会说第三件我思考很多的事情更多是关于文化和公司建设之类的。我们最近刚超过 200 人。我们增长非常快。到年底我们可能会达到 250 人。当你增长非常快时，你有 250 人都在试图弄清楚如何为 Modal 增加最大价值，并确保他们有正确的背景，有正确的动力，他们每天兴奋地来上班，因为他们能构建非常酷的东西，他们知道什么让 Modal 成功以及他们能做什么——对齐激励措施，确保人们有一种非常积极的文化，他们有那种隐式信任去做很多事情，但也有责任交付最好的东西，并对没有做到负责。对我来说，这些是在这个规模下超级关键的事情。当你只有 10、20、30 人时，大家可以坐在一个房间里，一切都是隐式的，你几乎能感觉到。人们能读懂我——他们能告诉我什么时候我有点烦。他们能看出我什么时候开心。现在我们 250 人，人们不一定看到这些，当然有很多新人可能有点紧张和 CEO 说话之类的。那么我如何保持平易近人？还有邓巴数，我认为那更多是假的——至少背后的故事——但它实际上还是有点真实，大概在 150、200 左右。我们正在奠定文化的基础，这非常非常重要。

turns.en: How many people are you guys trying to hire over the next year?
turns.zh: 你们明年打算招聘多少人？

turns.en: We've grown about 4x on an annualized basis in the last 12 months. I think that's an unsustainable growth rate on a relative basis. I've seen that you can double the team every year and that's not super hard to do. But what you start to see is cultural drift. You start to see islands of different working styles. You start to see people doing very speculative things. That's something I always watch out for in the engineering team. You go and talk to an engineer and I'm like, 'What are you working on?' And it turns out they're building something kind of fringe and is this really what you should spend time on? So growing very fast has that cost, and it has the cost of ramping people up. So I don't know, I think by the end of the year maybe 250, by the end of next year—we're going to keep growing like maybe 2.5x, 3x, so it's very likely we'll end up next year like 700 people or something like that.
turns.zh: 过去 12 个月，我们年化增长了约 4 倍。我认为相对而言这是不可持续的增长速度。我见过你可以每年让团队翻倍，那并不是特别难。但你开始看到文化漂移。你开始看到不同工作风格的孤岛。你开始看到人们做非常投机的事情。这是我在工程团队中一直警惕的。你去和工程师交谈，我问：“你在做什么？”结果他们在构建一些边缘的东西，这真的是你应该花时间做的吗？所以快速增长有那个代价，也有培养人员的代价。所以我不知道，我想今年年底可能 250 人，明年年底——我们会继续增长大概 2.5 倍、3 倍，所以很可能明年我们会达到 700 人左右。

turns.en: I'm going to assume most of those are engineers.
turns.zh: 我猜其中大多数是工程师。

turns.en: Mostly engineers, but also a lot of sales.
turns.zh: 主要是工程师，但也有很多销售。

turns.en: Okay. What kinds of engineers?
turns.zh: 好的。哪种工程师？

turns.en: It's primarily systems engineers. We've always been very deep into Linux and file systems and scalable systems and networking and cloud and stuff like that. So that's the core of what we're looking for—people who are really good at those things. We're also looking a lot at—because we moved up in the stack a little bit—we're doing a lot of work in the LM inference space. So now we're dealing with a separate set of concerns around CUDA and GPUs and MFU, like maxing out the tokens that you can get per GPU and a lot of those things. And even though I will say a lot of the work in that space in my opinion turns out to be more systems driven still, because it turns out KV caching and routing are actually still very systems-heavy problems. But yeah, a little bit more GPU performance and that kind of stuff. We're starting to build up a research team. We're very excited about moving into stuff around post-training and distillation and better methods for quantization.
turns.zh: 主要是系统工程师。我们一直深入 Linux、文件系统、可扩展系统、网络和云之类的东西。所以那是我们寻找的核心——真正擅长这些事情的人。我们也在大量寻找——因为我们向栈的上方移动了一点——我们在语言模型推理领域做了很多工作。所以现在我们处理一系列围绕 CUDA、GPU 和 MFU 的不同问题，比如最大化每个 GPU 能获得的 token 数量等等。而且尽管我会说，在我看来那个领域的很多工作仍然更多是系统驱动的，因为事实证明 KV 缓存和路由实际上仍然是非常系统密集型的问题。但是的，更多一点 GPU 性能之类的东西。我们开始建立一个研究团队。我们非常兴奋地进入后训练、蒸馏以及更好的量化方法等领域。

turns.en: For your customers or for internally?
turns.zh: 是为客户还是为内部？

turns.en: Both.
turns.zh: 两者都有。

turns.en: I think it's a little bit like with the FTEs. I think we initially will do a lot of stuff with our customers to optimize their models, but over time figure out how do we turn those into products. I think we'll arguably fail in a certain way if every time a customer needs to optimize a model we have to go and work with them. Long-term it has to be turned into products. So with the FDEs and with the research team, initially you're going to have to do a lot of work with the customers, and we are. But over time we're also building a lot of internal tooling and a lot of internal products that are fully self-serve. So we're working on a lot of stuff right now in the post-training space but also in the GPU performance space. So, a lot of cool stuff.
turns.zh: 我觉得这有点像 FTE 的情况。一开始我们会和客户一起做很多工作来优化他们的模型，但久而久之要想办法把这些变成产品。如果我们每次客户需要优化模型都得去和他们一起做，那可以说我们在某种程度上就失败了。长期来看必须把它变成产品。所以有了 FDE 和研究团队，一开始你得和客户做很多工作，我们正在这么做。但久而久之我们也在构建很多内部工具和很多完全自助式的内部产品。所以我们现在在后训练领域和 GPU 性能领域都在做很多工作。很多很酷的东西。

turns.en: Back to the product strategy stuff that you were talking about. What are your thoughts? What do we need over the next year, two years?
turns.zh: 回到你刚才说的产品策略。你怎么看？接下来一年、两年我们需要什么？

turns.en: I think it's incredibly hard to say, and if I said I know exactly what we need to build, I think I would be delusional. What we've seen so far, and what I kind of believe in on a more general level, is we need better building blocks. This is a new era of software, and we're unlocking a whole new type of applications that could not be built a few years ago. Doing all the GenAI stuff, code that LLMs output that needs to run in an isolated way—there are so many new primitives that are needed to work with GPUs and work with LLMs. We've built some building blocks so far, and that's unlocked a bunch of applications that the world has seen over the last few years, not just us, of course. But I think over the next few years there's going to be so many more cool things. I mentioned some stuff—I'm very bullish on training. I'm very bullish on batch jobs. I'm very bullish on certain things around agents and low latency and things like that. But in the end, we consider ourselves an infrastructure shop. We're not trying to build very narrow things. We try to build very general-purpose building blocks and put them in front of customers, and then those customers will combine those building blocks and build some incredible applications that we could have never anticipated.
turns.zh: 我觉得这非常难说，如果我说我确切知道我们需要构建什么，我觉得我就是在妄想。到目前为止我们看到的，以及我在更普遍层面上所相信的，是我们需要更好的构建模块。这是软件的新时代，我们正在解锁几年前根本无法构建的全新类型的应用。做所有 GenAI 的东西，LLM 输出的代码需要以隔离的方式运行——需要太多新的原语来与 GPU 和 LLM 协作。到目前为止我们已经构建了一些构建模块，这解锁了过去几年世界看到的一堆应用，当然不只是我们。但我认为未来几年会有更多酷炫的东西。我提到了一些——我非常看好训练。我非常看好批处理任务。我非常看好智能体和低延迟之类的某些东西。但最终，我们把自己视为一家基础设施公司。我们不是试图构建非常狭窄的东西。我们试图构建非常通用的构建模块，把它们放在客户面前，然后那些客户会组合这些构建模块，构建出我们根本无法预料的惊人应用。

turns.en: I want to go through some of your tweets. This will be the last part, and maybe you want to double-click on anything.
turns.zh: 我想过一遍你的一些推文。这会是最后一部分，也许你想深入聊聊任何内容。

turns.en: A lot of long-running persistent sandbox stuff right now. Today it feels lift-and-shift. I suspect sandboxes will evolve from devboxes in the cloud to something more ephemeral—one environment for every command and snapshotting in between so you can pause, resume, clone. Yeah, I mean we talked about this a lot.
turns.zh: 现在有很多关于长时间运行的持久沙盒的东西。今天感觉像是直接迁移。我怀疑沙盒会从云中的开发盒演变成更短暂的东西——每个命令一个环境，中间进行快照，这样你可以暂停、恢复、克隆。是的，我们谈过很多这个。

turns.en: Yeah, we talked a bit about it, right?
turns.zh: 是的，我们谈过一点，对吧？

turns.en: I'm fully—I think the median sandbox in Modal today is like 8 seconds long or something like that, which is kind of incredible when you think about it. And over time I think it might get even shorter. We want to support long-running sandboxes too. I think there are some very valid use cases around long-running sandboxes. But my vision is—the world needs also we need to figure out this: how can we just massively parallelize things and reduce the overhead of starting and stopping sandboxes.
turns.zh: 我完全——我认为今天 Modal 里沙盒的中位时长大概是 8 秒左右，想想都觉得不可思议。随着时间的推移，我认为它可能会变得更短。我们也想支持长时间运行的沙盒。我认为围绕长时间运行的沙盒有一些非常有效的用例。但我的愿景是——世界也需要我们弄清楚这一点：我们如何大规模并行化事物，并减少启动和停止沙盒的开销。

turns.en: I don't know if I ran an IPO-ready startup engaged in a capex arms race with a competitor, it would be nice to coordinate and pace the arms race a bit.
turns.zh: 我不知道如果我经营一家准备 IPO 的初创公司，与竞争对手展开资本支出军备竞赛，能稍微协调和调整军备竞赛的节奏就好了。

turns.en: No comment.
turns.zh: 无可奉告。

turns.en: The biggest downside of GPU scarcity is not that it's hard to get GPUs, but that almost all capacity is sold as three years—as a three-year rectangle starting 3 to 6 months in the future. That's not what demand looks like for most users. I think we talked about that a little bit as well.
turns.zh: GPU 稀缺的最大缺点不是很难获得 GPU，而是几乎所有容量都以三年期出售——作为一个三年期的矩形，从未来 3 到 6 个月开始。这不是大多数用户的需求形态。我想我们也谈过一点这个。

turns.en: Yeah. And you know, maybe just go a little bit deeper. One thing I think Modal has always been very, very good at is fully on-demand capacity, right? If a customer comes to us and needs 100 GPUs, we can typically give them that immediately. You don't even have to talk to a salesperson. And a lot of workloads in real life don't look like these flat, rectangular workloads. They scale up and down throughout the 24-hour cycle. They maybe grow over time. They maybe have certain burst periods. And to me that is a challenge with a lot of customers today. And I do think it's a legit problem for the space—the only prime way to get capacity is to buy these rectangular blocks. It's not great. I think the world needs to evolve, and that's fundamentally—I mean I'm very biased—but that's why I think Modal can play a very large role in that sort of duration transformation of offering more flexible capacity. And we can do that because we can aggregate many, many thousands of customers and the demand gets very smooth in aggregate. So that's a lot of the value prop of Modal—it's exactly that.
turns.zh: 是的。你知道，也许再深入一点。我认为 Modal 一直非常非常擅长的一件事就是完全按需的容量，对吧？如果客户来找我们需要 100 块 GPU，我们通常可以立即给他们。你甚至不需要和销售人员交谈。现实生活中的许多工作负载并不像这些平坦的矩形工作负载。它们在 24 小时周期内上下扩展。它们可能随时间增长。它们可能有某些突发期。对我来说，这是当今许多客户面临的挑战。我确实认为这是该领域的一个合理问题——获得容量的唯一主要方式是购买这些矩形块。这并不好。我认为世界需要进化，从根本上说——我的意思是，我很有偏见——但这就是为什么我认为 Modal 可以在这种持续时间转型中发挥非常大的作用，提供更灵活的容量。我们可以做到这一点，因为我们可以聚合成千上万的客户，需求在聚合后变得非常平滑。所以这就是 Modal 的很大一部分价值主张——正是如此。

turns.en: Would you say that's a differentiator? Oh really, okay.
turns.zh: 你会说这是一个差异化因素吗？哦真的，好的。

turns.en: Yeah, massive differentiator actually. In fact, I think Modal's—if you want to be very reductive—you can break down Modal's value prop into two things. One is the developer experience: the ability to iterate and build things and not have to think about infrastructure. The other thing is the capacity stuff. The more and more I think about Modal and where we're going in the long run, we're building—we're aggregating the world's compute capacity and we're very good at slicing it out very granularly because we built all this work around scaling up and down extremely fast, all the stuff around GPU snapshotting. We're working on some ways to make it much, much faster, and that model works at very large scale really, really well because you can aggregate lots of customers.
turns.zh: 是的，实际上是巨大的差异化因素。事实上，我认为 Modal 的——如果你想非常简化——你可以把 Modal 的价值主张分解为两件事。一是开发者体验：能够迭代和构建东西，而不必考虑基础设施。另一件事是容量方面的东西。我越是想 Modal 和我们的长期发展方向，我们正在构建——我们正在聚合世界的算力容量，我们非常擅长非常细粒度地切分它，因为我们围绕极快扩展和收缩构建了所有这些工作，所有围绕 GPU 快照的东西。我们正在研究一些方法让它快得多，而且这种模式在非常大的规模下运作得非常好，因为你可以聚合很多客户。

turns.en: Every month I keep saying our sandbox revenue might have plateaued, but it keeps going up 30% every month.
turns.zh: 每个月我一直在说我们的沙盒收入可能已经趋于平稳，但它每个月都在上涨 30%。

turns.en: It's kind of nuts. Like, I don't know, every month I'm like, well, you know, sandboxes grew a lot but clearly they kind of plateaued, and then they keep growing even more. So I don't know. And a lot of VCs, they're like, how did you know sandboxes was going to be big? And the truth is, I didn't. I thought it was going to be bigger than it was in 2023 for sure, but the fact that sandboxes is a third of our revenue today, it's insane. And you know, we're obviously very happy about it. We have a very large team investing in sandboxes.
turns.zh: 这有点疯狂。就像，我不知道，每个月我都觉得，嗯，你知道，沙盒增长了很多，但显然它们有点趋于平稳了，然后它们继续增长得更多。所以我不知道。很多风投，他们会说，你怎么知道沙盒会变大？事实是，我不知道。我确信它会比 2023 年更大，但沙盒今天占我们收入的三分之一，这太疯狂了。你知道，我们显然对此非常高兴。我们有一个非常大的团队在投资沙盒。

turns.en: You know, I don't want to trivialize it—we obviously want to give ourselves a lot of credit for seeing sandboxes for what it is today, a little bit back even in 2023. But I think I probably would have never taken a bet that revenue would be this large from sandboxes and the market demand would be so much.
turns.zh: 你知道，我不想轻描淡写——我们显然想给自己很多功劳，因为在 2023 年甚至更早一点就看到了沙盒今天的模样。但我想我可能永远不会押注说沙盒的收入会这么大、市场需求会这么多。

turns.en: There's an interesting structural reason why inference providers should exist separately from model builders. The best model keeps changing a lot. Inference providers can easily reallocate resources between models since overall demand is quite smooth.
turns.zh: 有一个有趣的结构性原因，说明为什么推理提供商应该与模型构建者分开存在。最好的模型一直在变。推理提供商可以轻松地在模型之间重新分配资源，因为总体需求相当平稳。

turns.en: So I mean if you think about all the Chinese labs and in the future hopefully more US labs too, every time a new lab releases the latest and greatest open source models, you see big shifts in demand for these models. And so I think a challenge is if all these labs independently held capacity, they would see when they launch a new model demand would go up a lot, and then another lab launches a better model and then the demand goes down.
turns.zh: 所以我的意思是，如果你想想所有中国实验室，未来希望还有更多美国实验室，每次一个新实验室发布最新最棒的开源模型，你都会看到对这些模型的需求发生巨大变化。所以我认为一个挑战是，如果所有这些实验室都独立持有容量，他们会看到：当他们发布新模型时需求会大幅上升，然后另一个实验室发布了更好的模型，需求就下降了。

turns.en: But of course in the background they're working on the next version, so I think there's a structural reason, like I said, why you're seeing demand shifting to the latest and greatest Chinese lab. I mean, it's not like everything just moves overnight, because a lot of models and prompts and stuff have a certain stickiness to it. But I do think there's an argument that it's very easy for a model—like right today we're running x number of thousand GPUs for one model, tomorrow we need to shift 50% of that to another model. Sure, that's what the system was built to handle. No one even needs to tell us to do that. It just magically does that.
turns.zh: 但当然，他们在后台正在开发下一个版本，所以我认为有一个结构性原因，就像我说的，为什么你会看到需求转向最新最棒的中国实验室。我的意思是，并不是一切都会一夜之间转移，因为很多模型和提示词等有一定的粘性。但我确实认为有一种论点，即对模型来说很容易——比如今天我们在为一个模型运行几千块 GPU，明天我们需要把其中 50% 转移到另一个模型。当然，这就是系统构建时要处理的事情。甚至不需要有人告诉我们去做。它就会神奇地做到。

turns.en: So you agree that basically the LLMs are commodities. And if you agree, then where do you think the business for the big labs is going to be?
turns.zh: 所以你同意基本上大语言模型是商品。如果你同意，那么你认为大实验室的业务将在哪里？

turns.en: I'm not sure if that's necessarily true, right? Like is Taylor Swift a commodity? Like she releases a big album and goes on a tour and makes a lot of money, and then there's a down year when she goes and records. I don't know if this is the best analogy, and then she releases a new album. So I don't know—she still has a lot of brand and there's a lot of power and makes a lot of margin. So as long as the labs repeatedly can launch new models and as long as the margin that they have on those models are such that they can pay off—amortize—the cost of training those models, it could still be a decent business I think.
turns.zh: 我不确定那是否一定正确，对吧？就像泰勒·斯威夫特是商品吗？她发行一张大专辑并巡演赚很多钱，然后有一年低谷期她去录音。我不知道这是不是最好的类比，然后她发行新专辑。所以我不知道——她仍然有很多品牌，有很大的影响力和很高的利润率。所以只要实验室能反复推出新模型，并且只要他们在这些模型上的利润率足以支付——摊销——训练这些模型的成本，我认为这仍然可能是一个不错的生意。

turns.en: So you don't think that the intelligence is plateauing?
turns.zh: 所以你不认为智能正在趋于平稳？

turns.en: No, I don't think so. I mean I think it remains to be seen, right? Like models today are very good at doing things that can be trained very efficiently using reinforcement learning. So we've seen that initially with coding and writing simple snippets. Over time, it's gotten really good at also writing production-level code. It's gotten really good at math. It's gotten really good at cybersecurity. Like these are all quite verifiable things. I still think it remains to be seen whether our models are going to be really good at cooking food or things that have more diffused targets and maybe longer feedback loops or whatever. I think humans—my feeling is we'll be quite good and quite competitive with models for a long time in those domains. But certainly AI models are getting very, very good, as I'm sure everyone can agree with.
turns.zh: 不，我不这么认为。我的意思是，我认为这还有待观察，对吧？就像今天的模型非常擅长做那些可以通过强化学习高效训练的事情。所以我们最初在编码和编写简单代码片段上看到了这一点。随着时间的推移，它在编写生产级代码方面也变得非常出色。它在数学方面变得非常出色。它在网络安全方面变得非常出色。这些都是非常可验证的事情。我仍然认为，我们的模型是否会在烹饪食物或那些目标更分散、反馈循环更长的事情上变得非常出色，还有待观察。我认为人类——我的感觉是，在这些领域，我们将在很长一段时间内与模型相比相当出色且具有竞争力。但当然，AI 模型正变得非常非常好，我相信每个人都会同意。

turns.en: Yeah. So obviously the models are getting really good at coding. They're already really good at coding. What other applications do you think maybe that aren't as big right now are going to become huge over the next few years?
turns.zh: 是的。所以显然模型在编码方面变得非常出色。它们已经在编码方面非常出色了。你认为还有哪些目前可能不那么大的应用会在未来几年变得巨大？

turns.en: I don't know, but I think anything that has a verifiable—computational bio, I think you mentioned.
turns.zh: 我不知道，但我认为任何具有可验证性的——计算生物学，我想你提到了。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Computational bio.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。计算生物学。

turns.en: I think those are not exactly verifiable, but there's certain ways you can run sim—you can use an LM to output predictions. Then you can do computational methods to simulate the molecular dynamics and get kind of feedback loops. I mean, I think material science is maybe another area where you have a little bit of that loop where you can synthetically manufacture certain materials and measure the properties and you just kind of put an agent in the loop and do things. So I have a physics background, I'm pretty excited about that. So drugs, materials, what else—drawing a blank, but I'm sure there's many other things.
turns.zh: 我认为那些并不完全是可验证的，但你可以通过某些方式运行模拟——你可以使用语言模型输出预测。然后你可以用计算方法模拟分子动力学，并获得某种反馈循环。我的意思是，我认为材料科学可能是另一个领域，你有一点那种循环，你可以合成制造某些材料并测量属性，你只需把一个智能体放入循环中并做事。所以我有物理学背景，我对此相当兴奋。所以药物、材料，还有什么——我一时想不起来了，但我相信还有很多其他事情。

turns.en: Cool. I mean those are all the questions that I had. Is there anything you wanted to talk about that I haven't?
turns.zh: 酷。我的意思是，这些就是所有的问题了。有没有什么你想谈但我没问到的？

turns.en: I'm good. This is great. This is a lot of fun.
turns.zh: 我很好。这很棒。这很有趣。

turns.en: Awesome. Thank you.
turns.zh: 太棒了。谢谢。

consensus.en: AI infrastructure must be rebuilt from scratch for GPU workloads, not wrapped over Kubernetes and Docker.
consensus.zh: AI 基础设施必须为 GPU 工作负载从零重建，而非在 Kubernetes 和 Docker 上简单封装。

consensus.en: Developer experience and agent experience share the same foundations: good docs, clear errors, fast feedback loops.
consensus.zh: 开发者体验与智能体体验共享相同基础：优质文档、清晰错误信息、快速反馈循环。

consensus.en: Sandboxes will evolve from lift-and-shift dev boxes to ephemeral, per-command environments with snapshotting.
consensus.zh: 沙盒将从“搬移开发机”演变为按命令临时创建、支持快照的环境。

consensus.en: Aggregating many customers smooths demand, enabling flexible on-demand capacity that rectangular three-year deals cannot.
consensus.zh: 聚合大量客户可平滑需求，提供三年期“矩形”合约无法实现的灵活按需算力。

consensus.en: Training is an underserved market, especially for smaller and midsize training runs, not just massive frontier runs.
consensus.zh: 训练是尚未充分服务的市场，尤其是中小规模训练，而不仅是大规模前沿训练。

consensus.en: Multi-tenant cloud is winning; on-prem reflects an outdated security model and limits product iteration speed.
consensus.zh: 多租户云正在胜出；本地部署反映过时的安全模型，并限制产品迭代速度。

contrarian.en: GPU supply is not fully cornered; if you pay enough, capacity is available, so buying everything is risky.
contrarian.zh: GPU 供应并未被完全垄断；只要出价够高就能获得算力，因此买断一切风险很大。

contrarian.en: Rising GPU prices are not necessarily bad; locked-in reservations benefit, while a price collapse would hurt buyers.
contrarian.zh: GPU 价格上涨未必是坏事；锁定预订者受益，而价格崩盘会伤害买家。

contrarian.en: Code reviews are largely optional; they often let people escape accountability, so invest more in CI/CD instead.
contrarian.zh: 代码审查基本是可选的；它常让人逃避责任，不如多投资 CI/CD。

contrarian.en: Agents may make cybersecurity safer overall, not just more dangerous, because they are good at finding and fixing vulnerabilities.
contrarian.zh: 智能体可能让网络安全整体更安全，而不仅是更危险，因为它们擅长发现和修复漏洞。

contrarian.en: Fine-tuning is no longer mandatory; open-source models are good enough off the shelf for many use cases.
contrarian.zh: 微调不再是必选项；开源模型开箱即用已足够好，能满足许多场景。

contrarian.en: The biggest downside of GPU scarcity is not difficulty getting GPUs, but that capacity is sold as three-year rectangles.
contrarian.zh: GPU 稀缺的最大弊端不是难获取，而是算力以三年期“矩形”合约出售。
